sourceInformation.source: Super Breakout (Atari, 1981 home version; original arcade game 1978).
sourceInformation.tech: Three.js r180 (0.180.0), WebGPURenderer with WebGPU and automatic WebGL 2 fallback; Rapier 2D 0.19.3; Gamepad API; Web Audio API; PeerJS 1.5.5; AI Hub Session Protocol 1, unmodified session client 1.4.0; HTML/CSS/JavaScript.
sourceInformation.artDirection: Cel-shaded extruded bricks, ink outlines, astronomical line art, warm paper, coral, mint, saffron and lilac. All scene art is code-generated geometry.
sourceInformation.animation: Three.js native AnimationMixer, AnimationClip and keyframe tracks for orbital drift, sector arrival, paddle squash and ink impact rings; procedural ball trails and debris.
sourceInformation.audio: All audio synthesized in code using Web Audio: 108 BPM orbital music, collision and menu effects, filtered Animalese-style gibberish crew voices. Music defaults to 10%. No audio files.
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub ghost score races for 1–4 players with progress, results and remote paddles. Standalone private PeerJS/WebRTC score races for 2–4 players. Same-device two-player cooperative campaign.
sourceInformation.testing: Headless Chromium 153 with software WebGPU and GPU pixel readback; deterministic Rapier full-campaign AI playthrough; scripted standard gamepad, keyboard, mouse and mobile touch controls; WebGL 2 visual checks at 1920×1080 and phone portrait; OfflineAudioContext signal checks; file:// startup with real CDN dependencies; real two-page PeerJS/WebRTC race, results and rematch; official AI Hub harness with two players, four players under 150 ms latency/50 ms jitter/5% loss, and host departure. Physical controller, human listening, real iOS and remote-network connectivity: unknown.
sourceInformation.research: Atari Super Breakout instruction manual: space-shuttle force-field premise, angle-based paddle returns, eight scoring rows, five serves, top-wall paddle shrink, Double, Cavity and Progressive variants, and eight programmed sound choices. Three.js r180 WebGPURenderer source, Rapier JavaScript documentation, PeerJS documentation, and AI Hub protocol/client/harness. Source has no character enemies; brick walls are the obstacles. Manual: https://atariage.com/2600/manuals_old/super_breakout.html . Hub: https://github.com/michaelcrosato/ai-hub/tree/main/lib/hub . Title chosen with node:crypto.randomInt from 50 silently brainstormed candidates: draw 23, Super Bounceout.
sourceInformation.environment: Codex CLI (headless); Linux, Ubuntu 26.04 on WSL2.

testingFeedback: 43 automated checks passed, including three official AI Hub harness scenarios. Testing caught 2 game issues: the stacked-paddle collision trap and an outline mesh covering brick faces. Both were fixed. Additional review corrected narrow-screen framing and completed online result/rematch controls.
1 critical game-breaking issue: an upward-moving ball could become trapped between the twin paddles, preventing the Cavity and Double stages from progressing.
The automated Rapier pilot played all four sectors to victory and verified captive-ball releases, POP hits, scoring, finite physics state and campaign progression. It exposed the stacked-paddle trap.

The first direct headless WebGPU screenshot was least useful because the compositor omitted the canvas. GPU pixel readback and screenshots through the engine’s WebGL 2 fallback gave useful evidence instead.
engineFeedback: Three.js made native animation tracks, orthographic 3D geometry and a consistent cel-shaded look straightforward. Rapier supplied real continuous collision detection and contact events.

I initially placed an ink backing mesh slightly in front of the coloured brick face and used two-sided paddle collision response. Visual and full-playthrough tests exposed both assumptions; depth ordering and one-way paddle contacts fixed them.
The complete game layer: paddle return rules, four stage variants, menus, input switching, procedural audio, attract AI and multiplayer lifecycle.
Coordinating fixed-step physics, arcade-directed paddle rebounds and animated rendering while preserving consistent controls across devices.
A simpler built-in path for combining WebGPU materials, ink outlines and screen-space effects would reduce setup.
promptFeedback: The source research, controller-first direction, attract mode and concrete shipping requirements made the intended experience clear.
The source year does not identify a platform; I used the 1981 home release and its manual. The relationship between standalone multiplayer and Hub multiplayer required a design choice.
Delivering a polished single-file game while verifying four source variants, three input families, synthesized sound and two multiplayer transports.
Specify the source platform and the required standalone online mode, and distinguish mandatory browser coverage from stand-in coverage.

aiHub.name: Super Bounceout
aiHub.description: A small ship meets a very colourful problem. Angle your paddle, time a perfect POP, free captive signals and break through four ink-drawn force fields, solo, with a couch crewmate or in an online score race.
aiHub.controls: Left stick / A,D / arrows / mouse / touch drag: move; Cross / A / Space / click / tap: serve and POP; Options / Esc: pause. Couch P2: arrows + Enter or second pad.
